motion: Homework should be banned in primary schools.

transcript.motion: Homework should be banned in primary schools.

turns.text: Homework at primary level crowds out play, family time and sleep, which are far more valuable for young learners. Children spend hours on repetitive worksheets that rarely deepen understanding and often just create stress at home. Teachers already assess progress during class, so take-home tasks are unnecessary. A ban would restore evenings to reading for pleasure, outdoor play and conversation, all of which build curiosity and confidence. Younger pupils need movement and rest, not more seatwork. The home should be a place of connection, not a second classroom. Banning homework respects childhood and trusts teachers to do their job during school hours.

The evidence does not support a blanket ban. A 2006 meta-analysis by Harris Cooper found a positive effect of homework on achievement, even in early grades, when it is short and purposeful. Homework also builds study habits and lets parents see what children are learning. In the 2019 TIMSS dataset, many high-performing systems used modest homework rather than none. A ban removes a tool that, used well, supports mastery in reading and maths. It also ignores differences among families: some parents rely on homework to spot difficulties early. Better policy is smart design, not prohibition.

My opponent cites averages, but averages hide harm. Even if scores rise slightly, children lose time for sleep, sport and family talk, which matter more at this age. A small gain on a test does not justify tired, anxious evenings. We should ask what kind of person we are raising, not just what kind of scorer. Homework also widens gaps, because some homes can help and some cannot. Teachers can notice struggles in class without sending sheets home. The right move is to protect childhood and trust classroom teaching, not to pile on more after the bell.

The pro side keeps saying play matters, but play and short tasks are not enemies. The Cooper review itself says the issue is quality, not existence. Countries that ban homework often see parents pay for private tutoring, which widens gaps more than school tasks do. A ban also removes a signal: when a child struggles with a reading log, parents and teachers learn early. If we care about equity, we should give schools clear guidance on short, feedback-rich tasks rather than eliminate a support that many families value and use to keep children on track.

The heart of this debate is simple. Young children need rest, play and time with the people who love them. Homework often turns evenings into battles over worksheets that add little to what good teaching already does. A ban sends a clear message: learning belongs in school, and home belongs to childhood. It also asks schools to be honest about what they can teach in the day. We can trust teachers, protect sleep, and let families read, talk and move together. That is a healthier start than any packet of tasks ever given to a tired eight-year-old.

The pro side wants to protect childhood, and I agree, but a ban is the wrong tool. The evidence points to short, purposeful tasks, not zero. The Cooper meta-analysis, TIMSS patterns, and the risk of private tutoring all show that prohibition can deepen gaps. A better motion would cap minutes, require feedback, and train teachers in design. That keeps play, sleep and family time while preserving a channel for parents to spot trouble. Reject the ban. Choose smart homework: brief, clear, useful, and monitored, so every child gets support without losing the childhood the pro side rightly values.
